definition: A linear polysaccharide of glucose units joined by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds that forms the load-bearing framework of plant cell walls and the main substance of cotton, flax and regenerated fibers.
explanation: Cellulose is an unbranched chain of D-glucose rings, each ring turned relative to its neighbor so that the chain lies flat and straight. Hydroxyl groups along every ring form hydrogen bonds within a chain and between neighboring chains, and stacked layers of chains are also held by van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions. The chains pack into microfibrils that contain both highly ordered and less ordered zones. In bast fibers such as flax, cellulose sits in a matrix of hemicellulose, pectin and a little lignin. Regenerated fibers such as viscose and lyocell are made by dissolving cellulose and re-forming it, which changes its crystal form and degree of order.
example: A student lays a linen thread and a viscose thread side by side and asks why they share so many behaviors, such as absorbing water readily and scorching rather than melting under an iron. Both are cellulose. The difference lies in how that cellulose is arranged: the linen keeps the native microfibril architecture grown by the plant, while the viscose has been dissolved and rebuilt into a new, less perfect structure.
caution: Cellulose names a molecule, not a particular fiber or an environmental profile. Cotton, linen, viscose, lyocell and paper all contain it, yet their morphology, chain length, crystal form and processing chemistry differ widely. Knowing that a fiber is cellulose-based does not tell you whether it is native or regenerated, how it was grown or pulped, or what solvents and finishes were used.
deeper: Each anhydroglucose unit carries three hydroxyl groups, at carbons 2, 3 and 6, and the beta configuration of the 1,4 linkage rotates successive rings by about 180 degrees, so the chain has a two-residue repeat corresponding to cellobiose. Dense intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding, together with van der Waals forces between stacked chains, locks chains into rigid microfibrils. Synchrotron X-ray and neutron fiber diffraction studies have mapped the chain packing and hydrogen-bonding network of the native cellulose I alpha form. Dissolving and regenerating cellulose, as in viscose or lyocell manufacture, converts it largely to a different crystal form, cellulose II. Because this bonding network is so extensive, cellulose decomposes before it melts, which is why regenerated cellulose fibers are spun from solution rather than from a melt. In flax, cellulose typically makes up roughly 64 to 78% of fiber mass.
origins: The French chemist Anselme Payen isolated cellulose in 1838 and recognized it as a common constituent of plant tissue. The name joins cell, from the Latin cellula (a small room), with -ose, the chemical suffix used for sugars, reflecting its location in cell walls and its glucose building blocks. The fine detail of its crystal structure took far longer to establish: the hydrogen-bonding patterns of native cellulose were resolved only with modern synchrotron and neutron diffraction.

definition: Colorfastness is a textile's resistance to change in its own color, and to transferring color onto other materials, under a defined exposure such as washing, light, rubbing or perspiration.
explanation: Fastness is always tied to a specific agent and test. Standard methods expose a specimen under controlled conditions, often alongside undyed adjacent fabric, then compare the result with reference standards. Two separate judgments are made: change in shade of the specimen, and staining of the adjacent fabric. Results are expressed as grades on a scale where 5 means no perceptible change and 1 means severe change, with half grades such as 3-4 used between steps. The international ISO 105 series and AATCC methods in the United States are the main frameworks.
example: A dark red cotton shirt is tested for rubbing: a white test cloth is rubbed across it dry and then wet. The dry test earns grade 4, the wet test grade 2-3. The shirt barely changes color, yet it can mark a light sofa or bag when damp. A single washing grade could not have predicted that: each agent needs its own test.
caution: A fastness grade applies only to the test method and conditions used; wash grades do not predict light or rubbing performance. Staining and change in shade are separate results. Grades are ordinal, not linear, so a 4 is not twice as good as a 2. Requirements vary by product and buyer, and a garment can be colorfast yet still shrink or pill.
deeper: Visual assessment uses grey scales, graded pairs of grey chips representing defined color differences, viewed under standardized lighting and geometry; separate scales exist for change in color and for staining. Lightfastness uses its own reference materials exposed alongside the specimen. Within ISO 105, parts are grouped by letter; for example, ISO 105-X12 covers color fastness to rubbing using a crockmeter. Instrumental grading converts measured color differences into grades, and research using spectral reconstruction and neural networks reports close agreement with trained visual assessors for rubbing stains. Dye chemistry drives outcomes: covalently bound reactive dyes resist washing, mordants improve natural dye fastness, disperse dyes on polyester need sublimation checks, and solution-dyed fibers often reach high grades because pigment is locked in the polymer.
origins: Fastness testing developed as dye chemistry multiplied and buyers needed common language for disputes over fading and bleeding. National textile chemists' associations and international standardization committees built methods and reference scales that could be reproduced between laboratories. Today laboratories commonly report ISO 105 or AATCC grades on test reports. Founding dates of specific organizations and methods were not verified for this edition.
